q: Which list contains the four government powers over private property?
options: Police power, eminent domain, taxation, escheat
Eminent domain, adverse possession, taxation, leasing
wrong: Appraisal, licensing, and recording aren't the four powers.
Adverse possession and leasing aren't government powers.
Partition and probate are court processes, not the four powers.
why: PETE: Police power, Eminent domain, Taxation, Escheat.
hook: PETE: Police, Eminent domain, Taxation, Escheat.

q: When the government takes private land for a new highway, it must pay:
wrong: Just compensation means fair market value, not assessed value.
The owner's debt doesn't set compensation.
why: Eminent domain requires public use and just compensation.
hook: Take it for the public, pay for it.

q: The legal process the government uses to exercise eminent domain is:
wrong: Escheat is for property without heirs.
why: Condemnation is how eminent domain is carried out.
hook: Condemn to take.

q: A person dies without a will and with no heirs. Their land:
options: Becomes public domain for anyone to claim
wrong: It goes to the state, not to anyone.
why: With no will and no heirs, property escheats to the state.
hook: No heir? The state is the heir.

q: Zoning and building codes are examples of:
options: Police power, which doesn't require compensation
wrong: Escheat is for property without heirs.
why: Police power lets government regulate for health and safety without paying owners.
hook: Regulate, don't pay.

q: A city installs new streetlights on one street and charges only the owners on that street. This is a:
wrong: Transfer taxes apply when property is sold.
Escheat is for property without heirs.
why: Owners who benefit from a specific improvement pay a special assessment.
hook: Special assessment: you benefit, you pay.

q: Property taxes are ad valorem, meaning they're based on value.
wrong: Ad valorem means according to value.
why: True.
hook: Ad valorem: by value.

q: Eminent domain can be used only for a public use or purpose.
wrong: Public use and just compensation are both required.
why: True.
hook: Take it for the public, pay for it.

q: A government dam project floods an owner's land repeatedly, but the government never formally condemned it. The owner may sue for:
wrong: Escheat is for property without heirs.
why: Inverse condemnation lets an owner seek compensation when government action effectively takes property.
hook: Inverse: the owner starts the taking case.

q: A new sidewalk costs $36 per front foot, split equally between the owner and the city. An owner has 80 front feet. What does the owner pay?
formula: Owner cost = front feet × cost per foot × owner's share
hook: Special assessment: you benefit, you pay.

q: An owner gets permission to build 3 feet closer to the side lot line than zoning allows, because the lot is oddly shaped. This is a:
wrong: A nonconforming use predates a zoning change.
A conditional use permit allows a special use, not a setback change.
why: A variance permits deviation from zoning requirements because of hardship.
hook: Variance bends the rule.

q: A gas station operating legally before its area was rezoned residential may continue as a:
wrong: Nothing was rezoned for one owner.
No special permit was needed; the use came first.
why: Uses that predate a zoning change are nonconforming and often allowed to continue.
hook: Nonconforming came first.

q: A church wants to build in a residential zone where churches are allowed only with approval and conditions. It needs a:
why: Uses allowed only with special approval need a conditional (special) use permit.
hook: Allowed with conditions: conditional use.

q: Zoning ordinances are the main tool for carrying out a community's:
why: The master plan sets the vision; zoning implements it.
hook: Plan the vision, zone the rules.

q: A newly built home can be lawfully occupied after the local government issues a:
wrong: A variance is a zoning exception.
The permit allows construction to start.
why: A certificate of occupancy confirms the building meets codes.
hook: Build with a permit, move in with a C of O.

q: A city rezones one lot in a residential area to commercial to benefit a council member's friend. This is:
wrong: A buffer separates incompatible uses for the public.
why: Singling out one parcel for a private benefit is spot zoning.
hook: One lot, one friend: spot zoning.

q: Major construction generally requires a building permit before work begins.
wrong: Permits let officials review and inspect.
why: True.
hook: No permit, no build.

q: Unpermitted additions are usually a matter for disclosure because they can affect value and insurability.
wrong: Buyers may face costs to permit or remove them.
why: True.
hook: No permit, disclose it.

q: A park placed between an industrial area and homes is an example of a:
wrong: Spot zoning benefits a single parcel.
A variance is an exception for one owner.
An easement is a use right.
why: Buffer zones separate incompatible uses.
hook: Buffer between neighbors who don't mix.

q: A lot is 70 feet wide. Zoning requires 7-foot side setbacks on each side. What is the maximum buildable width?
formula: Buildable width = lot width − (left setback + right setback)
why: Subtract both side setbacks: 56 feet.
hook: Subtract both sides.

q: Under CERCLA (Superfund), who can be liable for cleaning up contamination?
options: Current and past owners, even if they didn't cause it
Only the person who caused it
wrong: Liability reaches owners who didn't cause it.
why: CERCLA liability is strict and can fall on current and past owners.
hook: Buy the dirt, buy the dirt's problems.

q: A buyer of commercial land orders a Phase I environmental site assessment mainly to:
options: Identify likely contamination and support the innocent landowner defense
why: Phase I reviews history and records for contamination risk.
hook: Phase I: look before you're liable.

q: A buyer with a federally backed loan buys in a Special Flood Hazard Area. Generally the buyer must:
wrong: Elevation isn't required for existing homes to get the loan.
why: Federally backed loans in mapped high-risk flood zones require flood insurance.
hook: Flood zone plus federal loan equals flood insurance.

q: Filling wetlands generally requires a permit under the:
why: The Clean Water Act regulates filling wetlands, typically through the Army Corps of Engineers.
hook: Wet land, federal hand.

q: FEMA publishes the flood maps used to identify flood zones.
wrong: FEMA's flood insurance rate maps show flood zones.
why: True.
hook: FEMA maps the floods.

q: Superfund liability applies only to contamination caused after the buyer took title.
wrong: Liability can reach contamination that happened before the buyer owned it.
why: False.
hook: Buy the dirt, buy the dirt's problems.

q: Your client is buying an old dry-cleaning site. What should the agent do?
options: Recommend an environmental assessment by qualified professionals before closing
Tell them dry cleaners never cause problems
Ask the seller for an opinion and rely on it
wrong: Dry cleaners commonly used hazardous solvents.
Skipping due diligence risks huge cleanup liability.
The seller isn't an independent expert.
why: Environmental due diligence protects buyers from inherited cleanup costs.
hook: Phase I: look before you're liable.

q: A Special Flood Hazard Area is land with about what chance of flooding in any year?
why: SFHAs have a 1% annual chance of flooding, the so-called 100-year flood.
hook: 1% a year adds up.

q: A listing agent learns the home sits in a mapped flood zone. The agent should:
options: Disclose it as a material fact
Keep it quiet unless the lender raises it
Remove it from the MLS listing
wrong: Flood zone status affects costs and decisions.
That's a claim you can't support.
why: Flood zone status affects insurance costs and value, so it's material.
hook: Material: it could change the decision.

q: To claim the innocent landowner defense under CERCLA, a buyer generally needs to have done appropriate inquiry before buying.
wrong: All appropriate inquiry, like a Phase I, supports the defense.
why: True.
hook: Phase I: look before you're liable.

q: Recorded covenants, conditions and restrictions for a subdivision are known as:
why: CC&Rs are private rules recorded for a community.
hook: CC&Rs: private rules, recorded.

q: Zoning allows homes up to 35 feet tall, but the subdivision's CC&Rs limit homes to 25 feet. An owner may build:
wrong: The stricter private restriction still applies.
why: When public and private rules differ, the stricter one controls.
hook: Stricter rule wins.

q: The usual remedy for violating a restrictive covenant is:
wrong: Forfeiture is the remedy for a condition, not a covenant.
Escheat is for property without heirs.
why: Courts enforce covenants with injunctions or damages.
hook: Covenant: court order.

q: An old deed restriction bans sales to people of a certain race. Today it is:
wrong: No one can enforce a discriminatory restriction.
why: Discriminatory restrictions violate fair housing law and can't be enforced.
hook: Discrimination can't be recorded into law.

q: Who typically enforces CC&Rs in a planned community?
why: HOAs enforce their own recorded rules, along with owners in some cases.
hook: The HOA enforces the CC&Rs.

q: Recorded CC&Rs bind future owners of the property.
wrong: Recorded restrictions generally run with the land.
why: True.
hook: CC&Rs: private rules, recorded.

q: Violating a deed condition, as opposed to a covenant, can cause the owner to lose title.
wrong: Conditions carry forfeiture as a possible remedy.
why: True.
hook: Condition: you could lose it.

q: Your buyer plans to park a boat in the driveway of a home in an HOA community. What should the agent do?
options: Have the buyer review the CC&Rs and rules, which may restrict boats, before removing contingencies
Tell them HOAs never restrict boats
Tell them zoning allows boats, so it's fine
Ask the seller whether it's allowed
wrong: Many HOAs restrict boats and RVs.
The seller's opinion isn't the governing document.
why: The governing documents decide; the buyer should read them.
hook: Read the rules before you buy.

q: A limit on use written into a specific deed, like "no commercial use," is a:
wrong: A variance is a zoning exception.
An easement in gross gives a use right.
why: Private use limits in a deed are deed restrictions.
hook: Written in the deed, binding on the owner.

q: An HOA ignored dozens of violations of a fence rule for years, then sues one owner. The owner's best argument may be that the HOA:
options: Waived or abandoned enforcement through its long, selective inaction
wrong: The CC&Rs exist; the issue is enforcement.
Permits don't relate to the HOA's claim.
why: Selective, long-term failure to enforce can support defenses like waiver or laches.
hook: Enforce it consistently or risk losing it.
